checks.label: The waveform for power is always positive, never negative, for a resistive circuit, so power is never returned to the source as it is with reactive loads: in step (0°) the drawn power wave never dips below the line, and at every other angle from −90° to 90° part of it does

Capacitors and inductors absorb energy from the circuit during one half-cycle and then discharge it back to the circuit during the other half-cycle: at 90° (a coil) and −90° (a capacitor) the drawn power wave is above the line for as many instants as below it, and averages 0 W

The average power can be expressed as P avg = V I cos φ: at every angle from −90° to 90° the average of the drawn power wave, sampled instant by instant, equals 70.7 V × 7.07 A × cos φ, as do the dashed line and the triangle's floor, and so on every other load drawn

The actual amount of power being used, or dissipated, in a circuit is called true power, measured in watts, P: on lesson 6's bench only the resistor dissipates it, 2² × 6 = 24 W, and on the mains coil 5² × 40 = 1000 W

This phantom power is called reactive power, measured in volt-amps-reactive (var), with the symbol Q: on lesson 6's bench the coil's 2² × 8 = 32 var, on the scrubber at 60° 433 var, and at resonance the coil's 250 var and the capacitor's cancel to 0 var

Because true power and apparent power form the adjacent and hypotenuse sides of a right triangle, the power factor is also equal to the cosine of the phase angle: on every screen, and at every angle on the sliding screens, the drawn triangle closes with P² + Q² = S² and P ÷ S = cos φ

Any power factor less than 1 means that the wiring has to carry more current than would be necessary with zero reactance: with true power held at 500 W, the current is 7.07 A rms in step and more at every other angle, 14.1 A rms (20 A peak) at 60°, where S = 1000 VA, Q = 866 var and the cable bar shows 4 times the heater's heat

UK mains electricity operates at a nominal voltage of 230V: on 230 V, lesson 6's coil at 5 A takes 1000 W of 1150 VA, with 568 var, a power factor of 0.87 and φ = 29.6°, and the motor at 10 A takes 1600 W of 2300 VA, a power factor of 0.70, with 1652 var at 45.9°

Known answers: at 60° the power wave runs from 750 W to −250 W around 250 W; its in-step part peaks at 5 A with humps to 500 W averaging 250 W, its quarter-cycle part at 8.66 A with a 433 W slosh averaging 0 W; 4.8 kW of 6 kVA leaves 3.6 kvar; the slips give 375 W, 756 W and 1323 W; 30° ahead gives 433 W, −250 var, 0.87 and a dip to −67 W; S stays 500 VA at every angle
On the average puzzle a right answer shades the area above the dashed 250 W line and the gap below it, and the two are equal, as an average makes them

Lesson 6's impedance triangle times the current squared, 2² = 4, is the power triangle: the drawn sides start as 6, 8 and 10 Ω and end as 24 W, 32 var and 40 VA at the same 53.13°, and each part's meters agree, 12 V × 2 A, 16 V × 2 A and 20 V × 2 A
Each puzzle accepts only its right answer; before an answer its picture hides what is asked, a right answer draws it, and each wrong pick with a drawing draws what it claims, in red
Every demonstration has finished arriving within 4.5 s of its screen opening, none starting before the 0.35 s screen fade ends; every answer's motion, right or wrong, within 2.5 s
